As long as the airplane existed only “as a design,” its hypothesis could either be examined internally or compared with sensory experience.
Everything still took place, so to speak, inside the human being. There was no possibility of confronting the hypothesis directly with objective reality.

But once the airplane was built, work—the real, physical effort of the workers—carried the hypothesis beyond the boundaries of human thought and inserted it into reality itself, which exists independently of that thought.
The built airplane is, on the one hand, just as objectively real and independent of the human mind as a mountain, a cloud, or a plant.
On the other hand, no airplane would ever have appeared on Earth without a design: without a hypothesis that exists only in and through human beings.
This is precisely what characterizes human work.
Something ideal—a design, a hypothesis, a theorem, and ultimately some form of discourse or logos—is transformed, through a series of real actions, into something real and material: a thing.
Through work, discourse becomes part of the real world.
Work therefore allows us to compare discourse not merely with subjective experience but with objective reality itself.
In other words, it allows us to establish its objective truth.
A design for an airplane contains a whole range of theories: mathematical, mechanical, physical, and chemical.
And the fact that an airplane constructed on the basis of those theories actually flies proves their truth.

Suppose an engineer had designed an airplane on the basis of theories claiming that the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees, that action is not equal to reaction, that the volume of a gas is not inversely proportional to pressure, or that carbon does not combine with oxygen. His machine would never have left the ground.
The fact that the airplane does fly therefore shows that the theories underlying its design correspond to reality. In that sense, they are true.
We might even say that the confrontation between theory and reality, and thus the establishment of truth, takes place without human intervention. Reality itself passes judgment.
Living nature, so to speak, eliminates its own unsuccessful designs. It kills malformed organisms at birth and allows species that are badly adapted to their environment to die out.
In the same way, the natural world as a whole eliminates a failed airplane design.

Conversely, a design successfully realized through work—a successful and therefore true design—becomes part of the real world. As a reality, as something “objective,” it is no different from the world’s “natural” components.
So, in practice, a theory embodied in an airplane that actually flies is just as “absolutely” true as a theory corresponding to any natural phenomenon.
There is, however, one crucial difference.
We have no direct way of establishing which of our theories actually corresponds to “natural” reality. But we know perfectly well which theory was used to construct a particular airplane.
Since sensory experience can unquestionably distort reality, comparing a theory with sensory experience can never give us a complete guarantee of its truth.
Only comparison with reality itself can do that.
But such a comparison can be established only when the relevant reality is itself created through work on the basis of the theory whose truth we want to test.
Truth is therefore established neither rationalistically nor empirically. It is established experimentally or technically.
We do not rely only on the human ability to speak and to have sensory experiences. We also make use of the human ability to work.
I would like to call the theory of knowledge that takes the fact of work into account and seeks the criterion of truth in experiment or technique “experimentalism” or “technicism.”
We have seen that only technicism can explain how truth is possible and rescue it from scepticism.
Of course, knowledge verified experimentally or technically remains partial. But within those limits it is nevertheless fully and definitively—absolutely—true.
It can therefore already be regarded as part of an ever-expanding omniscience whose possible scope has no limit.
There is, however, an important qualification.
The fact that an airplane flies confirms the truth of all the theories involved in its design, but it does not establish the truth of each individual element taken separately.
We can, of course, vary the conditions of an experiment and in this way isolate particular aspects of the knowledge being tested.
But every experiment rests on such an enormous number of theoretical assumptions that it is simply impossible to verify a completely isolated theoretical proposition by technical means.

Strictly speaking, every technical experiment tests the whole body of knowledge currently available about the natural world. It even tests propositions of which we may not yet be fully conscious, because they function only as “tacit” assumptions of the experiment.
The success of our technology therefore shows that we do in fact possess some true knowledge of the natural world.
But much of that knowledge has not yet been formulated. It does not yet exist for us as explicit knowledge.
The theories we have formulated are therefore only parts of a larger verified whole. Detached from that whole, they may turn out to be false.
Our airplane provides a simple illustration.
The design that enables us to build a functioning airplane is very far from being a complete theory of that airplane.
It tells us how to construct the machine. But it says nothing about the metal from which the airplane is made or the fuel on which it runs.
Yet the fact that the airplane flies confirms not only our mechanics but also the physical and chemical theories concerning its metal and its fuel.
Most of these theories, however, have still not been fully formulated. This is especially true of knowledge that remains largely “empirical,” such as our knowledge of the strength of metals.
It is therefore perfectly possible that some of our explicit, partial theories about metals happen to work in the particular case of this airplane while being false when treated as general theories.

In short, the complete theory of anything produced by technology—like the complete theory of any concrete reality—is nothing less than omniscience, or at least complete knowledge of the whole natural world.
The actual existence of the technically produced thing demonstrates the absolute truth of that complete knowledge.
But because what we actually possess is only partial knowledge, we have no guarantee that every part of it is absolutely true.
Some elements of our partial knowledge may fail to belong to true omniscience at all. In other words, some of them may be false.
We are therefore once again led to the conclusion that, in the fullest sense of the word, we can truly know only when we know everything.
Yet, as we have just seen, we know only what we know how to make technically.
So until we have learned how to create everything, we will know nothing with absolute certainty.
Today we know enough to build machines. That is why our knowledge of mechanics seems to be our most certain knowledge.
But even the most complex machine is very simple compared with a “natural” thing. Our mechanical knowledge is therefore only a tiny and extremely elementary part of our knowledge of nature.
We do know how to transform one chemical compound into another and, in the simplest cases, how to “make” compounds from their elements.
But these attempts are still at an early stage.

We may be able to transform one element into another. But we are technically incapable of “making” those elements from electrons. And creating a living organism from chemical compounds lies further beyond our present abilities still.
Taken together, this shows just how imperfect our knowledge of nature remains—how uncertain it is and how much of it is still open to doubt.

Yet the productivity of human work and the successes of technology are facts. They show that our knowledge already contains something unconditionally true and that we are genuinely moving toward perfect knowledge: toward omniscience.
In other words, the very existence of work and technology allows us to say with confidence that the human aspiration to omniscience—that is, philosophy—is neither absurd nor doomed to failure.
Partial knowledge of nature that can be tested experimentally and technically can be regarded as an embryo of omniscience and, in that sense, as philosophical knowledge.
Like all scientific knowledge, such knowledge is still abstract when taken by itself.
But concretely speaking, there is no natural world existing purely “in itself.” What concretely exists is a world known by human beings who live and work within it.
When philosophy studies concrete reality, therefore, it does not study the natural world in isolation. It studies human knowledge of that world.

And because this knowledge is genuinely true to some extent and can be expanded without any fixed limit, knowledge of this knowledge can itself be regarded as a path toward true omniscience—that is, as philosophy.
For this to happen, philosophy need only recognize that the truth of our knowledge of the world is guaranteed solely by work and technology.
When philosophy explains how the concrete world is organized—a world in which human beings know what they know—it must also recognize the presence of technical work within that world.
As a theory of our knowledge of the natural world, philosophy must therefore also be a theory of work and technology.
But philosophy, as potential omniscience, is not only knowledge of human knowledge of nature—and therefore an indirect knowledge of nature itself.
It is also, and perhaps above all, knowledge of the knowledge that human beings have of themselves. It is therefore knowledge of the human being itself.
It is easy to see that neither rationalism nor even empiricism can explain how knowledge of human beings can attain truth. In this respect they fail just as they failed with knowledge of nature.
Here too, however, scepticism can be avoided if we adopt the standpoint of experimentalism and take account not only of the cognitive and contemplative side of human life but also of its active side.

For if the truth of our knowledge of nature can be guaranteed only through work or technology, then it is not difficult to show that the truth of our knowledge of humanity can be established only through social and political struggle—through “politics” in the broadest sense.

A theory that human beings formulate about themselves, about their specifically human life—that is, about their social, political, and historical existence—must also be carried beyond the limits of subjective experience and confronted with the most objective historical reality.
In other words, the theory itself must be transformed into historical reality.
And transforming an ideal existence into a real existence always requires effort. It requires action that is both conscious and real.

When the real, conscious effort that realizes a theory about nature takes the form of technical work, the corresponding effort that realizes a theory about human beings can only take the form of political struggle.
Ultimately, the only guarantee that some knowledge of humanity is true is the actual existence of a society and a state founded on that knowledge.
If we attempt to establish a state on a false conception of human beings, that state will sooner or later—and inevitably—collapse.
The stable and lasting existence of a state can therefore be said to demonstrate the truth of the ideas on which it rests.
Testing political knowledge is, in this respect, broadly similar to testing technical knowledge.
On the one hand, as long as a state is not universal, the knowledge that it “guarantees” can only be partial.
Yet every state is made, so to speak, out of human beings. It is created by human beings on the basis of some conception of what a human being is.
The existence of any state therefore always guarantees the truth of some part of humanity’s knowledge of itself.
On the other hand, a state, like a technology, provides only a holistic verification of its theoretical assumptions, most of which have not yet been explicitly formulated.
For that reason, only omniscience about humanity could count here as absolutely true.
And such omniscience could in turn be guaranteed only by a state that genuinely encompassed every aspect of human existence.
As a natural being, a human being can reproduce, like any other living organism.
But human beings do not yet know how technically to “make” individuals through work—that is, to “reproduce” them on the basis of a theoretical knowledge of their animal life.
Our knowledge of that aspect of ourselves therefore still cannot be regarded as absolutely true.
